rejected.title: Formal and informal register
card: Register is how formal or informal language is. Writers and speakers choose it to suit their audience, purpose and setting.
Formal
full sentences, careful word choices and no slang. It suits a speech to a school assembly, a letter to a principal or an essay.
Informal
relaxed words, slang, short forms such as can't, and sometimes incomplete sentences. It suits a chat or text message with friends.
Using the wrong register can sound out of place. Slang in a job application can seem careless, and stiff language in a chat with friends can seem odd.
rejected.remember: Choose a register to fit your audience, purpose and setting.

a.q: Which sentence uses the most formal register?
opts: I am writing to request permission to attend the excursion
Hey, can I come on the excursion or what
Any chance I could tag along on the excursion
Pretty keen to go on the excursion, so yeah
a.why: The sentence that requests permission to attend uses full, careful wording with no slang or short forms. The others use casual phrases such as hey, tag along and yeah, which are informal.
a.clue: Look for careful wording and no slang.

b.q: Jai is writing to the principal to ask for a new bike shelter. Which opening suits his audience best?
opts: Dear Ms Nguyen, I am writing to propose a new bike shelter
Hey Ms Nguyen, we really need a bike shelter, mate
Yo, bikes get soaked here, so build us a shelter
G'day, how about a shelter for bikes, yeah
b.why: A letter to a principal calls for a formal register. The opening that starts with Dear Ms Nguyen has a polite greeting and full, careful wording. The others use slang such as hey, mate, yo and yeah, which suits friends, not a principal.
b.clue: Think about who will read the letter.
